doc.title: Dorothy Donegan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Playing the White House: screening, Rosemary Clooney and a standing ovation
summary: She followed Rosemary Clooney, played everything in ten minutes, stole the show before Herbie Hancock, and says the TV exposure mattered more than her colleagues.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans

blocks.x: Oh my. When you arrived in Washington DC, did they have a car waiting for you?
Yeah, the Secret Service met us and took us to the Capitol Hotel. And old Herbie Hancock was there, Wynton Marsalis, and Joshua Redman and Red Mitchell. Everybody.
They were all there. So, they picked you up in the hotel and took you to the White House. Did they make you have credentials or something you had to show?
You had to go through a screening.
What kind of screening?
Oh, they took your fingerprints and everything.
Oh they did? Then, would they take you into the dining room or did they make you wait in the anteroom?
I guess anteroom.
Until your turn?
Yes.
So, who came on first?
I don’t know.
When did you play?
I followed Rosemary Clooney. And then Herbie Hancock had to follow me.
He had to follow you?
He was disgusted. His lip dropped down to his thing.
What did you choose to play for the President?
They only gave me 10 minutes, so I played everything I knew in 10 minutes.
Did the President look pleased?
Yeah, I got a standing ovation.
Marvelous.
And Bobby McFerrin, they were all frowning.
Why were they frowning?
I got that standing ovation, they couldn’t top that. USA Today says, “You stole the show, thanks, you stole the show.” And they all stood up. I was all by myself.
What did you do, take a bow?
Yes, I bowed to the President, then I bowed to Hillary.
Wonderful. So, you think that was about the high point of your career?
I think so. It sounds like a closer.
You could still have a movie, you know, of your life.
When you gonna do that?
Miss Donegan, can you tell me why the celebration at the White House was so important to you? Why was that the high point?
Well people all over the country saw it. They call you up. They don’t call you ‘til they see you on TV.
How about the presence of your musical colleagues, there, was that important to you?
Not really, ‘cause they don’t want me on the bill anyway and I know it. So, I had to get on the bill and get my money and get out. ‘Cause Herbie Hancock wants to run everything.
(laughs)
